strengths: The active-set ghost reformulation is an interesting and potentially useful way to combine finite-difference hypergradients with mature black-box convex solvers. The solver-agnostic motivation is practically significant.

For linear constraints under stable active-set identification, LICQ, strong convexity, and sufficient smoothness, the proposed local reduction appears plausible and offers a meaningful alternative to differentiating a KKT system.

The evaluation covers QP, Sudoku, and SOCP settings and includes useful ablations on dimension, solver tolerance, batch size, gradient agreement, runtime, and memory. The reported training convergence and speedups are promising.

The paper is generally organized and readable, relates the method to recent differentiable-optimization and bilevel work, and includes an appropriate impact statement without evident unresolved ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The central guarantees do not follow from the stated assumptions. Lemma C.1 additionally assumes twice-continuous differentiability and strong regularity, and its O(delta) remainder appears to require stronger Lipschitz derivative conditions. Theorem 4.6/C.2 nevertheless invokes only Assumptions 4.2–4.3, asserts that both problems are well-conditioned, and concludes logarithmic complexity without establishing the missing regularity uniformly.

The general-convex extension is not technically convincing. Assumption D.1 postulates an oracle returning accurate primal and dual solutions with the correct active set—the difficult capability the method is meant to provide—so Corollary D.5 is an oracle result rather than an implementable first-order complexity result. Moreover, its proof is largely deferred to an assertion that all terms are O(epsilon).

There is a concrete error in Lemma D.2: from ||B†|| <= C_B one obtains sigma_min(B) >= 1/C_B, so the perturbation threshold and resulting pseudoinverse bound should scale as 1/(2C_B) and 2C_B, respectively. The manuscript instead uses C_B/2 and 2/C_B. This invalidates the displayed argument as written.

The active set is defined using both zero slack and strictly positive multipliers, effectively requiring strict complementarity in addition to local constancy. Weakly active constraints and active-set transitions are central difficulties, yet the main theorem does not state strict complementarity clearly. Appendix F instead guarantees stationarity for a smoothed, different objective and therefore does not recover the main claim.

The claimed O(log(1/epsilon)) cost is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1 says to use “any solver,” omits the required O(epsilon^2) inner accuracy from C.2, and does not identify an algorithm or count the work required to obtain primal-dual solutions and correctly identify the active set. Describing this as near-constant time overstates what is proved.

The experimental evidence does not isolate the differentiation method fairly: methods use different solvers and modeling stacks, BPQP is reimplemented by the authors, and no matched-backend comparison is supplied despite solver agnosticism being a headline claim. Feasibility residuals, active-set accuracy, confidence intervals over the stated ten seeds, and test-set performance are also absent.

Several empirical conclusions are stronger than the evidence. “Sublinear” dimension scaling is inferred from a few wall-clock measurements rather than derived, and the memory discussion is internally inconsistent: experiments are described as CPU-only, but Appendix G reports “GPU memory,” with plotted usage approaching 500 GB despite a stated 384 GB allocation.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The source-code sentence contains no URL, while essential details such as learning rates, batch sizes, MLP widths, data-generation distributions, QP/SOCP matrices, exact solver backends and versions, perturbation selection, and active-set thresholds are missing. Consequently, the substantial runtime and memory claims cannot presently be independently verified.

Presentation has numerous correctness-affecting inconsistencies, including Theorem 4.6 stating O(log(1/epsilon)) while Theorem C.2 states soft-O(1), incomplete or self-referential proof text in Appendix D, and typographical problems in figures and captions. Overall, the promising idea is outweighed by gaps in the central theory and insufficiently controlled, non-reproducible empirical support.

strengths: Originality/significance: The active-set “ghost” reformulation combined with finite-difference hypergradients is an interesting attempt to make differentiable convex optimization solver-agnostic and first-order. If validated, avoiding explicit KKT factorizations could be useful for large optimization layers.

Soundness: The linear-constraint development contains a plausible core idea, and the paper explicitly identifies LICQ, strong convexity, and active-set identification as important conditions rather than concealing them.

Evaluation: The manuscript examines QP, Sudoku, and SOCP layers; compares against several relevant methods; reports ten seeds; and includes useful ablations on dimension, solver tolerance, batching, gradient similarity, and memory. Presentation/ethics: The motivating bottleneck and high-level algorithm are reasonably easy to follow. The impact statement appropriately notes that downstream objectives and constraints require domain-specific validation, and I found no major unresolved ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness: The advertised general-convex-constraint result is not established at an acceptable level. Appendix D contains apparent pseudoinverse/conditioning errors: from ||B†||≤C_B one obtains a lower singular-value bound of 1/C_B, but Lemma D.2 instead treats C_B as that singular-value bound and concludes ||B̃†||≤2/C_B. The associated perturbation threshold is correspondingly inverted. The appendix then dismisses the crucial derivative comparison with one sentence and even says to compare “Appendix D.2 and Appendix D.2.” These gaps directly undermine Corollary D.5 and the paper's broad general-convex claim.

Soundness: The O(log(1/epsilon)) theorem rests on unusually strong access assumptions: the approximate primal-dual solve must identify the exact active set, including multiplier status, at every queried point. Algorithm 1 merely says to use “any solver” and gives no implementable identification rule or robustness margin. Near degenerate constraints this information is precisely what an approximate solver cannot reliably supply. Appendix F acknowledges the problem, but its smoothing theorem concerns a modified objective and does not validate the main algorithm on the stated problem.

Soundness/presentation: Several theorem statements suppress assumptions used in their proofs. Lemma C.1 additionally requires twice-continuous differentiability and strong regularity of the ghost KKT system, while Theorem 4.6 is stated only under Assumptions 4.2–4.3. The proof of Theorem C.2 further asserts without a complete derivation that both primal problems are “well-conditioned” and attain the necessary solution and dual accuracy in logarithmic time. Constants and conditioning dependence hidden by O-notation are important here, so describing the cost as near-constant “time” overstates what is shown.

Soundness: The cone-constraint discussion is only a short informal indicator-function linearization and does not constitute a rigorous extension to SOCPs. Consequently, the SOCP experiment does not by itself support the corresponding theoretical scope.

Evaluation: Runtime comparisons confound the proposed differentiation principle with different modeling stacks, canonicalization costs, solver backends, and specialized implementations (SCS, qpsolver, diffcp, GUROBI, and an unspecified QP closed form). There is no controlled comparison using matched forward solvers, so the attribution of speedups to the first-order oracle is not convincing.

Evaluation: The baseline protocol is unclear and potentially unfavorable to LPGD. The main text says LPGD is reported at the same tolerance as the proposed method even though that tolerance is said to be insufficient for convergence, whereas the appendix says 1e-12 is required and dramatically slower. It is unclear which setting underlies each headline timing. Alt-Diff is omitted solely because it was slow, without even a small-scale quantitative comparison.

Evaluation/presentation: Despite claiming ten seeds, the plots show no confidence intervals or numerical tables, leaving variance and statistical reliability unreported. Claims of “sublinear” scaling are inferred from a small range of empirical dimensions rather than supported by a dimension-dependent complexity analysis. Gradient accuracy is measured against CvxpyLayer as a proxy rather than a verified reference.

Reproducibility: The abstract leaves the source-code URL blank. Essential details—including learning rates, batch sizes, epochs/stopping criteria, perturbation selection, active-set thresholds, random-instance distributions, precise solver configurations, and raw numerical results—are absent. The hardware/memory reporting is also inconsistent: experiments are described as CPU-only with 384 GB total memory, while the appendix calls the measurements GPU memory and plots values approaching 500 GB.

Significance/originality: The work is closely built on the finite-difference/meta-algorithmic framework of Kornowski et al. (2024), with active-set reduction providing the main new step. That could be a useful specialized contribution, but the exact-active-set requirement substantially narrows applicability, the general-convex extension is presently unsupported, and evaluation is limited to synthetic tasks plus Sudoku. These issues prevent the claimed broadly scalable drop-in layer from being established.

Overall: There is a promising linear-constraint idea, but central theoretical scope, experimental attribution, and reproducibility all have material deficiencies. Substantial correction and stronger controlled evidence are required before others could reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Originality: The active-set ghost reformulation is a creative way to reduce inequality-constrained differentiation locally to an equality-constrained problem. Coupling this with a perturbed lower-level solve yields a practically attractive, solver-agnostic alternative to KKT differentiation.

Significance: A differentiable optimization layer that avoids forming or factorizing Hessian/KKT systems could be useful for large structured problems. The drop-in CVXPY/PyTorch interface and support for general convex solvers increase the potential impact.

Soundness: The manuscript provides a meaningful theoretical framework, including local active-set equivalence, finite-difference hypergradient analysis, an overall Goldstein-stationarity result, and discussion of why active-set information is necessary. The appendix contains substantial proof material rather than relying only on intuition.

Empirical evidence is reasonably broad: synthetic decision-focused learning, Sudoku, and SOCP experiments compare against CvxpyLayer, QPTH, LPGD, BPQP, and dQP. The paper also studies dimension scaling, memory, gradient similarity, solver tolerance, batching, and GPU QPTH.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The main construction is motivated effectively, and the distinction between the general convex implementation and the QP specialization is understandable.
The impact statement appropriately notes that downstream objectives and constraints require domain-specific validation; no material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The strongest guarantees rely on a demanding active-set-identification assumption. Correctly identifying constraints with positive multipliers from approximate primal-dual solutions can itself be difficult, particularly near active-set transitions or without a quantitative strict-complementarity margin. Appendix F explains why some such condition is needed, but this still substantially limits the headline applicability.

The general nonlinear-convex-constraint extension is less constructive than the main text suggests. Assumption D.1 directly grants an approximate primal-dual oracle that returns the same active set, and the authors acknowledge that they do not know an algorithm with the required dual convergence. Consequently, the general-constraint complexity result partly transfers the central computational difficulty into an oracle assumption.

Theorem 4.6 is stated under Assumptions 4.2 and 4.3, whereas its supporting argument invokes additional regularity and conditioning: Lemma C.1 assumes twice continuous differentiability and strong regularity of the KKT system, while Appendix A introduces Hessian-smoothness constants not clearly included in Assumption 4.2. The theorem statement should explicitly collect all assumptions and make constant/condition-number dependence visible.

The claimed O(log(1/epsilon)) cost is not fully justified at the implementation level. The proof asserts that accurate primal solutions are obtained in logarithmic time because the problems are well conditioned, while Algorithm 1 allows “any solver” and includes an original inequality-constrained solve. The oracle model, projection/constraint-processing costs, warm starts, and costs of active-set and dual recovery need clearer accounting.

The runtime comparison confounds differentiation strategy with solver and canonicalization choices: FFOCP uses SCS, CvxpyLayer uses diffcp, FFOQP uses qpsolvers, and dQP uses GUROBI. Thus the results establish strong end-to-end performance for the implementations, but do not cleanly isolate the benefit of the proposed backward estimator. Same-forward-solver comparisons or controlled backward-only benchmarks would strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix reports ten seeds, dataset size, dimensions, tolerances, and hardware allocation, but omits important numerical details such as learning rates, batch sizes, epoch counts, full data-generation distributions, solver versions/options, and uncertainty intervals. The manuscript’s source-code URL is blank in the provided version, and most plots lack error bars or numerical tables.

There is an apparent reporting inconsistency: Section 6 says all methods run on CPU, whereas the memory appendix describes peak GPU memory despite allocating hundreds of GB of CPU memory. The memory measurement methodology and the unusually large values should be clarified.

Some empirical claims are stronger than the displayed evidence supports. In particular, “sublinear” runtime scaling is inferred from a small finite range rather than established asymptotically, gradient similarity degrades and becomes noisy later in training, and the evaluation uses only three mostly synthetic or structured benchmarks. Performance at active-set transitions and under degeneracy is not directly examined.

Overall, the paper presents a promising and potentially useful contribution, but the acceptance case is borderline because the scope of the headline theoretical guarantees is narrower than the framing and the empirical/reproducibility details need tightening. I lean weak accept given the novel construction, substantial analysis, and encouraging experiments.
